segments.t: Arkady has left the square, with his wife Vika beside him. Last time, he promised a lecturer to save an old monastery wall, then quietly told his deputy to get rid of her. Now his phone rings, and he greets the caller as Viktor Stepanovich, an important official, though the voice on the line doesn't sound much like a Viktor. Let's listen in Russian first.
А мою жизнь лучше сделать не хочешь?
Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
Но вечером я обещал быть с женой.
Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
Не надо кричать. Хорошо, я буду сегодня.
Let's go through it. Arkady answers the phone in his most official voice.
'Viktor Stepanovich, greetings.' "Privetstvuyu vas" ('I greet you') sounds stiffly official — put on for Vika sitting right beside him. The caller is far less formal.
'Hi, Arkady Borisovich.' Mixing casual "privet" ('hi') with formal "Arkady Borisovich" already hints this is no ordinary boss. Then comes a simple question.
'What are you doing?' "Delayesh" carries the familiar 'you' inside its '-esh' ending, so no pronoun is needed. Arkady answers like a politician.
'Working. Making people's lives better.' Again "rabotayu" and "delayu" skip 'I' because the '-u/-yu' endings already say it. The caller has a better idea.
А мою жизнь лучше сделать не хочешь?

'And you don't want to make my life better?' Putting "moyu zhizn" ('my life') right at the front contrasts her with 'people's lives', ending on "ne khochesh?" ('don't you want?'). Arkady keeps up the act.
Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
'Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.' "Nikak" before "ne mogu" means 'in no way at all', turning 'I can't' into 'there's zero chance'. He adds a reason.
'There's a lot of work.' Literally 'of work, very much' — after "mnogo" ('a lot'), "rabota" shifts its ending to "raboty". The caller doesn't give up.
'Well, come in the evening.' "Priyezzhay" specifically means 'come over by transport or car', unlike coming on foot. Arkady tries another excuse.
Но вечером я обещал быть с женой.
'But I promised to be with my wife this evening.' "Obeshchal" ('promised') is the male speaker's form, and "s zhenoy" means 'with my wife'. Now the caller sulks.
'Well, if you don't want to, suit yourself.' "Ne khochesh, kak khochesh" — 'don't want to, as you want' — is a classic Russian shrug when someone turns you down. Then comes a little threat.
Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
'I'll have a good time on my own.' Listen to "sama" ('myself' or 'on my own'): that '-a' ending belongs to a female speaker, giving away 'Viktor Stepanovich' at once!
Не надо кричать. Хорошо, я буду сегодня.
'There's no need to shout. All right, I'll be there tonight.' "Ya budu" ('I'll be') often stands in for 'I'll show up' or 'I'll be there'. Then he hangs up like a businessman.
'Right, cheers then.' "Zhmu ruku" literally says 'I shake your hand', a brisk man-to-man sign-off used to fool Vika. She is curious.
'And?' Two tiny words, "i chto?" — literally 'and what?' — ask 'so what did he want?'. Arkady has his cover story ready.
'He's called an emergency meeting.' "Naznachil" ('he scheduled') uses the male form to keep up the fiction that a man called it.
'So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?' Literally, 'so, not to wait for you today?' — "tebya ne zhdat?" asks 'should I?' using the simplest version.
'No, darling, don't wait.' "Milaya" ('sweetheart' or 'darling') is the feminine pet word, followed by "ne zhdi" ('don't wait'). He sighs as if it's a sacrifice.
'I need to do a bit of work.' tucking "nado" ('need to') right at the end of "porabotat nemnogo nado" makes it sound weary and reluctant. Here's the whole conversation once more.
А мою жизнь лучше сделать не хочешь?
Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
Но вечером я обещал быть с женой.
Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
Не надо кричать. Хорошо, я буду сегодня.
So the busy mayor has a late meeting tonight, and it isn't with Viktor Stepanovich. Listen for 'I really can't today' when you watch. See you next time!
